Smote
smōt
v. (past tense of smite; rendering Hebrew nakah, Greek epataxen)
The past tense of smite, from Saxon smitan, to strike. The verb survives in English chiefly through the Authorized Version, and it covers everything from a blow of the hand to the destruction of an army, from a plague to the striking of a conscience.

Biblical Definition

Smote is the past of smite, to strike, and Hebrew nakah ranges across every degree of the action. It records the ordinary language of ancient warfare: “Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword” (Joshua 11:10); “David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah” (2 Samuel 8:3). It records the plagues on Egypt: “He smote their vines also and their fig trees; and brake the trees of their coasts” (Psalm 105:33). And in one of the smallest and sharpest uses in Scripture, it records God's dealing with a prophet's comfort: “God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered” (Jonah 4:7). The whole force of Jonah's book turns on that verse. God, who had spared a city of six-score thousand persons, takes away one plant, and the prophet who begrudged mercy to Nineveh grieves bitterly for a gourd he neither made nor tended.

Webster 1828 Definition

The past tense of smite, to strike; used of blows, of battle, of plague, and of God's direct action. In Scripture it ranges from the smiting of kings and armies to the worm that smote Jonah's gourd.

expand to see more

SMOTE, v. [Sax. smitan.] The past tense of smite; to have struck.

2. To strike with the hand, a weapon, or an instrument; to give a blow to.

3. To kill; to destroy the life of, by a weapon or by a stroke.

4. To afflict; to chasten; to punish; as, God smote the land with a plague.

5. In Scripture, smote the king thereof with the sword, Josh. 11; it smote the gourd that it withered, Jonah 4.

Key Scripture

Joshua 11:10 — "And Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms."

2 Samuel 8:3 — "David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates."

Psalm 105:33 — "He smote their vines also and their fig trees; and brake the trees of their coasts."

Jonah 4:7 — "But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered."

Modern Corruption

The conquest narratives are treated by modern readers either as an embarrassment to be explained away or as a licence for present-day violence. Both misread them: they record a unique judicial act of God against specific nations, executed by a covenant people under direct command, and never repeated.

expand to see more

The moral objection assumes the Canaanites were dispossessed arbitrarily. Scripture says otherwise and says it early: God tells Abraham that his descendants will not return for four generations, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full — four centuries of forbearance before judgment. Leviticus 18 catalogues the practices for which the land spued out its inhabitants, including the burning of children, and warns Israel in the same breath that the land will do the same to her. That warning was executed: Israel herself was smitten and exiled for the same offences. The conquest is judgment, not ethnic preference.

The abuse in the other direction is more urgent, because it is not merely academic. No nation, army, or movement today holds the commission Joshua held. The conquest was a unique, bounded, divinely commanded act within redemptive history, and the New Testament transfers the warfare entirely: our weapons are not carnal, and the sword the church wields is the word of God. The magistrate bears a real sword under Romans 13, for the punishment of evildoers within his own sphere, and that is a different thing altogether. Anyone reasoning from Joshua 11 to a present-day campaign has misread both testaments.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nakah covers the whole range of striking — a blow, a wound, a defeat, a plague. Greek patasso is to strike or smite, used of the shepherd smitten in Zechariah's prophecy and of the angel striking Herod.

expand to see more

Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to strike, smite, wound, kill; the single verb behind nearly every English smote.

Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — a plague or slaughter; the noun of the same root, of God's striking.

Greek patasso (G3960) — to strike, smite; used in I will smite the shepherd, quoted by Christ.

Hebrew qiqayon (H7021) — the gourd or plant prepared for Jonah and then smitten by the worm.

Saxon smitan — to strike, to smear; the root of the English verb.

Usage

"Of the conquest under Joshua: took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword (Joshua 11:10)."

"Of the plagues upon Egypt: He smote their vines also and their fig trees (Psalm 105:33)."

"Of a prophet's comfort taken away to teach him mercy: it smote the gourd that it withered (Jonah 4:7)."
